1Part 1

What makes a nutrient essential?

An element is essential if it meets any of these three tests. Decide which test each piece of evidence shows.

1The plant cannot complete its life cycle without the element.
2No other element can substitute for its action.
3It is part of a metabolic pathway or required by an essential enzyme.
2Part 2

What is a plant made of?

The chart shows typical concentrations of each essential element in plant dry matter. Start on the linear scale, then switch to the log scale and compare.

Hover or tap a bar to see its value.

Typical values, % of dry weight (Epstein, 1972). Real plants vary by species and growing conditions.

3Part 3

Liebig's Law of the Minimum

Each stave is one nutrient, set as a percent of what the crop needs. The barrel only holds water up to its shortest stave, just as growth is limited by the scarcest nutrient. The sliders start at a grower's soil test.

Drag to turn the barrel.

4Part 4

Getting nutrients to the root

Nutrients reach the root surface three ways: root interception, mass flow with water, and diffusion. The chart shows the share each method supplies for a corn crop.

Data from Barber, S.A. 1984. Soil Nutrient Bioavailability. John Wiley & Sons.

Mass flow model

Water evaporates out of the leaves (transpiration). That pulls more water from the soil into the root, and dissolved nitrate rides along with it. The root spends no energy on this step.

water (H₂O)nitrate (NO₃⁻)
Transpiration
Water flow to root
Nitrate reaching root
5Part 5

Crossing the membrane

The inside of a root cell is negatively charged. That charge pulls positive ions (cations) in and pushes negative ions (anions) away. Pick an ion, set its concentration in the soil water, and see whether it can flow in passively through a channel or needs active transport through a carrier powered by the H⁺ gradient.

SOIL WATERCYTOPLASM

Inside the cell
Ion's balance point
Cell membrane
Uptake

Simplified model at 25 °C using typical cytoplasm concentrations. The balance point is the membrane voltage at which the concentration push and the charge pull cancel out (the Nernst potential). If the real membrane is more negative than that point for a cation, or more positive for an anion, the ion can flow in on its own.
